name: Westinghouse WGen7500DF
summary: A 7,500-watt dual fuel portable with remote start and a 30-amp L14-30R, sized for a 1/2 to 1 HP well pump plus essentials through a transfer switch.
verdict:
The WGen7500DF is the generator most well owners should shortlist first. It has the right size and the right outlet for a typical submersible pump plus kitchen and lighting circuits.

**The 240V outlet is the point.** Westinghouse rates it at 7,500 running and 9,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 6,750 running and 8,550 peak on propane. The panel has two GFCI duplex outlets and a 120/240V 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/), which feeds a power inlet and a [transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/) or interlock. That 240V connection is what most submersible pumps need.

**Size it to your pump.** A 1/2 or 3/4 HP pump is comfortably inside its starting capacity, and a typical 1 HP pump is within reach if the fridge and freezer are not starting at the same moment. On propane, plan your list around 6,750 running watts, not the gasoline figure.

**Fuel flexibility.** The 420cc engine draws from a 6.6-gallon tank, with up to 11 hours on gasoline and up to 8 hours on a 20 lb propane cylinder. Propane keeps for years, so you can store it instead of rotating stabilized gasoline. Key-fob remote start saves a trip out in the rain. It weighs 201 lb, so it needs its wheels and a level spot.

Owners report easy starts and steady power for pumps; the common complaint is open-frame noise. It is the top pick in our [generator for well pump](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) guide. For a 50-amp outlet and more headroom, see the [WGen9500DF](/gear/westinghouse-wgen9500df/).

faqs.q: Can the Westinghouse WGen7500DF run a 1 HP well pump?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. A 1 HP 240V submersible typically needs about 1,000 running watts and a few thousand watts to start, inside the 9,500 peak watts on gasoline and 8,550 on propane. Connect through the L14-30R and a transfer switch, start the pump before the fridge and freezer, and check your pump maker's starting figure for 1.5 HP and up.

faqs.q: WGen7500DF vs WGen9500DF: which should you buy?
faqs.a: The [WGen9500DF](/gear/westinghouse-wgen9500df/) adds 2,000 running watts on gasoline, 1,750 on propane, and a 50-amp 14-50R outlet, for larger pumps or a window AC on top of essentials. The WGen7500DF is lighter at 201 lb versus 211 lb and enough for a 1 HP pump plus a fridge, freezer and lights. Buy the smaller one unless your load list needs more.

name: DuroMax XP13000EH
summary: A 13,000-watt dual fuel portable with 50-amp and 30-amp 240V outlets, for 1.5 HP well pumps or homes that start several motors at once.
verdict:
Buy the XP13000EH when your pump is 1.5 HP or larger, or when the well has to start while the rest of the house is running. It is the most output in this group, with a small propane penalty.

**The headroom.** DuroMax rates it at 10,500 running and 13,000 peak watts on gasoline, and 9,975 running and 12,350 peak on propane, from a 500cc engine. That is only a 5% drop on propane. The extra surge means the generator's voltage dips less when a pump motor's locked-rotor current hits, which is easier on the pump.

**Two 240V outlets.** The panel has a 120/240V 50-amp outlet and a 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/), plus a 120V 30-amp twist-lock and two GFCI duplexes. A 30-amp, 240V circuit carries at most 7,200 watts, so use the 50-amp outlet with a 50-amp inlet like the [Reliance PBN50](/gear/reliance-pbn50/) and an interlock to use the full rating.

**Fuel and weight.** DuroMax lists 8.5 hours at half load on gasoline and 6.5 hours on propane. It weighs 248 lb, so it needs its wheel kit and a good surface, and it burns noticeably more fuel than a 7,500-watt unit.

Owners report it starts big pumps without drama and holds voltage well; the common complaints are weight and noise. It ranks in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) and [generator for well pump](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) guides.

faqs.a: Often, yes. A 2 HP 240V submersible can need several thousand watts to start, and the XP13000EH offers 13,000 peak watts on gasoline and 12,350 on propane. Connect through the 50-amp outlet and a matching inlet, start the pump with other motors off, and confirm your pump maker's starting figure before you rely on it.

faqs.q: XP13000EH vs XP12000EH: is the bigger one worth it?
faqs.a: For big pumps or several motors, yes. The XP13000EH adds 1,000 running watts on gasoline, 10,500 versus 9,500, and about 950 on propane, 9,975 versus 9,025, from a 500cc engine instead of 457cc. Both have 50-amp outlets. If your list fits under 9,000 watts, the [XP12000EH](/gear/duromax-xp12000eh/) saves weight and fuel.

name: Champion 9000W Dual Fuel (100155)
summary: Champion’s 9,000-watt peak dual fuel portable with electric start and a 120/240V locking outlet, a value pick for well owners with 1/2 to 1 HP pumps.
verdict:
Champion's 9,000-watt [dual fuel](/glossary/dual-fuel/) generator is a value pick for well owners: big starting watts, two fuels and a 120/240V locking outlet in a mid-range tier. The figures here come from the manual for model 100155; Champion has refreshed this family, so match the model number on the listing.

**Starting watts are the headline.** Champion rates it at 9,000 peak and 7,000 running watts on gasoline, and 8,100 peak and 6,300 running on propane, from a 439cc engine. For a 1/2 or 3/4 HP submersible on a 240V circuit, that is ample surge. A 1 HP pump should work if you let it start before the fridge and freezer circuits come on.

**The 240V outlet.** The 120/240V locking outlet feeds a power inlet and a [transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/), which is how a 240V pump gets power. A 30-amp, 240V connection can carry up to 7,200 watts, more than the 7,000 running watts the generator makes on gasoline.

**Fuel and weight.** The 6.1-gallon tank is smaller than most rivals here, so expect more refills on gasoline; propane lets you store fuel that does not go stale. Net weight is 202 lb, so it lives on its wheels. Like the other open-frame units here, it is loud and must run outdoors.

Owners report reliable starts and good value; the common complaint is the small tank. It appears in our [generator for well pump](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) guide. For more running watts, compare the [Champion 9200 Dual Fuel](/gear/champion-9200-dual-fuel/).

Connect it through the 120/240V locking outlet and a transfer switch, start the pump first, then add the fridge and freezer. Check the pump maker's starting figure for 1.5 HP and up.

faqs.q: Champion 9000W vs 9200W Dual Fuel: what is the difference?
faqs.a: The [9200W](/gear/champion-9200-dual-fuel/) is the bigger, newer unit: 9,200 running watts on gasoline versus 7,000, a 459cc engine versus 439cc, a 7.7-gallon tank versus 6.1, plus CO Shield shutoff and a 14-50R outlet. The 9000W (100155) is enough for a pump and essentials, but the 9200W is the better buy if both are available.

name: Westinghouse WGen9500DF
summary: A 9,500-watt dual fuel portable that keeps 8,500 running watts on propane, with remote start and both 30-amp and 50-amp outlets, the best all-round dual fuel pick.
verdict:
The WGen9500DF is the dual fuel generator most buyers should start with, because it loses less on propane than most rivals. That matters, since the reason to buy dual fuel is to run on propane when gas stations are dark.

**The propane number.** Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 running and 12,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 8,500 running and 11,200 peak on propane, a drop of about 10%. Many open-frame units give up 15% or more. At 8,500 watts on propane you can run a fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace blower, lights and a window AC with staggered starts.

**Both 240V outlets.** The panel carries two GFCI duplex outlets, a 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/) and a 50-amp 14-50R. A 30-amp, 240V circuit tops out at 7,200 watts, so use the 14-50R with a 50-amp inlet and interlock to tap the full output.

**Runtime and size.** Westinghouse lists about 8 hours on gasoline from the 6.6-gallon tank and 7 hours on a 20 lb propane cylinder at half load. It has electric, recoil and key-fob remote start. The trade-offs are 211 lb of dry weight and a 74 dBA rating. The standard model has no CO shutoff; the WGen9500DFc adds a CO sensor, and that is the version to look for.

Owners report easy remote starts and strong propane output; the common complaint is weight. It is the top pick in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guide and appears in our [best RV generator](/best-rv-generator/) guide. Run your list through the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/) first.

faqs.a: Yes. A 13,500 BTU rooftop AC typically runs at about 1,300 to 1,800 watts and needs a few thousand watts to start, well within 8,500 running and 11,200 peak watts on propane. The 14-50R matches a 50-amp RV cord. For a 30-amp RV with a TT-30 inlet, use a properly rated adapter.

name: Champion 9200W Dual Fuel (201302)
summary: Champion’s 9,200-watt dual fuel portable with CO Shield, a 7.7-gallon tank and both 30-amp and 50-amp outlets, the value pick for whole-home essentials.
verdict:
This is the dual fuel generator most people should price first, and it is the top portable in our home outage guide. It packs big output, CO shutoff and a large tank into a mid-range tier.

**Build your list from propane.** Champion rates it at 9,200 running and 11,500 starting watts on gasoline from a 459cc engine, and 8,280 running and 10,350 starting on propane. That covers a refrigerator, a freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, lights and Wi-Fi together, with room for a window AC if you stagger starts. Size with the propane figure, since that is the fuel you will lean on in a long outage.

**Runtime.** The 7.7-gallon tank gives about 10 hours at half load on gasoline. On propane, Champion lists about 5 hours at half load, so plan on several 20 lb cylinders a day or a larger tank.

**Outlets and safety.** The panel has GFCI household outlets, a 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/) and a 14-50R that Champion caps at 38 amps. CO Shield shuts the engine off if carbon monoxide builds up, a backup to good placement; see [CO shutoff](/glossary/co-shutoff/). It weighs 209 lb and is rated at 74 dBA.

Owners report reliable starts and good value; the common complaint is short propane runtime on a 20 lb cylinder. It ranks in our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) and [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guides. Check the model number, since Champion also sells gasoline-only 9,200-watt units.

name: Generac GP7500E Dual Fuel

Not every house needs 9,000-plus watts, and the GP7500E Dual Fuel is the pick for the many that do not. It is the mid-size choice in our dual fuel guide.

**The ratings.** Generac rates it at 7,500 running and 9,400 starting watts on gasoline, and 6,800 running and 8,500 starting on propane. That covers a refrigerator, a freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, lights and a window AC with sensible staggering. Generac's PowerRush feature is designed to boost starting capacity for motor loads like pumps and compressors.

**Runtime and safety.** Generac lists up to 10 hours at half load on gasoline from a 7.9-gallon tank, and 5 hours on a 20 lb propane cylinder. COsense monitors carbon monoxide around the unit and shuts it down if levels climb; see [CO shutoff](/glossary/co-shutoff/) for how these systems work.

**Transfer switch ready.** The panel has two GFCI duplex outlets and a 120/240V 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/), which matches a standard 30-amp manual switch such as the [Reliance 31406CRK](/gear/reliance-31406crk/). What you give up is a 50-amp outlet and the extra headroom of the 9,500-watt class. It weighs 204 lb.

Owners report easy starts and like the CO protection; the common complaint is weight for a 7,500-watt unit. It appears in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guide. If your load list fits under about 6,500 watts on propane, it is the simpler buy.

name: Westinghouse WGen6000DFc
amazonQuery: Westinghouse WGen6000DFc EFI dual fuel generator
summary: A 6,000-watt EFI dual fuel portable with a CO sensor and long listed runtime, for homes whose essentials fit under about 5,000 watts on propane.
verdict:
The WGen6000DFc is a smart mid-size dual fuel pick if your essentials are modest and you care about runtime. Electronic fuel injection and a CO sensor make it more modern than most open-frame units this size.

**The ratings.** Westinghouse rates it at 6,000 running and 7,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 5,400 running and 6,750 peak on propane. That covers a fridge, freezer, sump pump, gas furnace blower, lights and internet, with room for one more motor if you stagger starts. Check your list with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

**EFI stretches fuel.** The 274cc engine uses electronic fuel injection instead of a carburetor, so there is no carburetor bowl to gum up between outages. Westinghouse lists up to 14 hours on the 4.75-gallon tank and up to 9.5 hours on a 20 lb propane cylinder. Those are best-case figures at light load; heavy loads cut them.

**Safety and hookup.** The CO sensor shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up, a backup to safe placement rather than a substitute; see [CO shutoff](/glossary/co-shutoff/). Westinghouse lists 120/240V output, so it can feed a 30-amp [transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/) through a power inlet, and remote electric start saves a trip outside.

Owners report easy starts and good fuel economy; the common complaint is that it runs out of headroom with a well pump plus other motors. For more power, step up to the [WGen7500DF](/gear/westinghouse-wgen7500df/), or compare picks in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guide.

name: DuroMax XP5500EH
summary: A compact 5,500-watt dual fuel portable with electric start, for budget essentials backup: fridge, sump pump, lights and internet on gasoline or propane.
verdict:
The XP5500EH is a budget way into dual fuel. It will not run a well pump plus a houseful of motors, but it handles the core essentials and lets you store propane instead of gasoline.

**The ratings.** DuroMax rates it at 4,500 running and 5,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 4,275 running and 5,225 peak on propane, from a 224cc engine. That is only a 5% loss on propane. A fridge at about 700 running watts, a sump pump, a few lights, a TV and internet fit inside 4,275 watts with room to spare. A window AC may fit if nothing else large is starting.

**Size is the appeal.** Retail listings put it at about 124 lb, far lighter than the 200-lb-plus big portables, and it has electric start with recoil backup. The tank holds about 4 gallons, and DuroMax lists about 8 to 9 hours at half load on gasoline.

**Know the limits.** At 4,500 running watts you will need to choose loads and start motors one at a time. It is an open-frame unit, so it is louder than an [inverter generator](/glossary/inverter-generator/) and must run outdoors, well away from windows.

Owners report easy starts and good value; the common complaint is noise. For more headroom on [dual fuel](/glossary/dual-fuel/), step up to the [Westinghouse WGen6000DFc](/gear/westinghouse-wgen6000dfc/), or see the larger picks in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guide.
